Below is a concise breakdown of each demonstration, separating the core physical principle involved from the step-by-step actions:

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Demo 1
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Key Physical Principle:  
  – A side-hinged window that pivots about its vertical hinge axis once the latch or handle is disengaged.

• Sequence of Actions:  
  1. Turn the window’s handle partly to unlatch.  
  2. Push the window outward on its side hinge.  
  3. Continue pushing until the window is fully open (about 90 degrees).


────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Demo 2
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Key Physical Principle:  
  – A lever-controlled reclining mechanism that locks into discrete positions (ratchet-style).  
  – The backrest can only tilt as far as surrounding obstacles allow.

• Sequence of Actions:  
  1. Pull the recline lever to the first click, tilting the backrest about 30 degrees.  
  2. Attempt a second pull to recline further.  
  3. Stop because the backrest impacts the wall.  
  4. Return to the first recline position to avoid hitting the wall.


────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Demo 3
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Key Physical Principle:  
  – A horizontally sliding window mounted on a track, allowing linear (side-to-side) motion instead of pivoting.

• Sequence of Actions:  
  1. Grip the window frame on one side.  
  2. Push (or pull) the sash along the horizontal track.  
  3. Slide it open until the desired gap is achieved, creating an opening on the opposite side.


────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Demo 4
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Key Physical Principle:  
  – A crank-handle mechanism linked to a scissor arm, which pushes or pulls the window outward from its bottom edge as the handle is turned.

• Sequence of Actions:  
  1. Turn the crank handle clockwise.  
  2. The scissor arm gradually extends.  
  3. The bottom of the window pivots outward, opening the window as the arm expands.

stage1.probe_response:
From the mechanical behavior and sensor readings, the window’s tilt-and-turn lever settles into two “clicked” (detent) positions. The first is around 45° from vertical, which prepares the window for a side-swing (casement) opening; the second is at about 135°, which tilts the sash inward from the top.

In practice:  
• 45° Detent (first “click”): The sash is held on its vertical hinges, allowing it to swing open into the room if you pull it correctly from the side. However, our exploration showed that pulling at the top or bottom edges wouldn’t swing it open—those edges remain locked. You would need to grasp the sash nearer the handle side (or the frame opposite the hinge) to pivot it inward.  
• 135° Detent (second “click”): The sash tilts in from the top on the horizontal upper brackets. This gives you a smaller ventilation gap at the top edge without fully swinging the sash into the room.

Regarding the environment: because there is a table with breakable items (vase, plant, book) less than a meter away from the window, the wide side-swing mode risks knocking into them unless they are moved or the window is opened gently from an angle that clears the table. The tilt mode, on the other hand, opens only at the top and avoids colliding with anything on the table.

tool_selection.full_response:
(1) Demo 2 is most relevant because it illustrates using a lever to set a tilt angle and then stopping or reverting when an obstacle is encountered—matching our goal to open the window at a limited tilt angle so it will not collide with the table or objects on top.

(2) I will employ a “tilt mode” opening technique, analogous to how Demo 2 used partial reclines and stops. This means rotating the handle to the 135° detent and pulling the top edge in just enough for ventilation.

(3) From exploration, we know that at handle 135° the top brackets engage a hinge axis on the horizontal supports, allowing an 8° inward tilt without contacting the table or its items. The force-displacement data confirmed no collision at that angle.

(4) Execution Plan:
  • NAVIGATE_TO[window] – Position the manipulator at the window’s handle.  
  • TWIST[handle, 135] – Turn the handle from 0° to 135° to engage tilt mode.  
  • NEW_ACTION[tilt_inward, manual_force, window_top] – Gently pull the window’s top edge until a safe 8–10 cm gap is open.  
  • Release input force, ensuring the window rests in its locked tilt position.  
  • Confirm clearance over the table by visually verifying no collisions.  

SELECTED_TOOL: technique_B

stage3.probe_response:
My plan did work as expected. I successfully placed the window handle at the 135° tilt position and pulled the top edge in just enough for ventilation without disturbing any nearby objects. Here is a breakdown of what went well, what did not, and lessons for next time:

• What succeeded:
  – Tilting the window at 135° allowed fresh air in through the top and avoided contact with the coffee table and its items.  
  – The hinge and handle mechanics behaved as predicted from the exploration phase, so the sash opened smoothly and locked into the tilt position.  
  – The objects on the table (vase, pot plant, and book) stayed safely untouched thanks to the limited tilt angle.

• What failed or caused difficulty:
  – There was no direct “failure,” but I was not able to test the full side‐swing mode within the exploration phase because pulling at the window’s bottom edge did not disengage from the sill. Based on the sensor data, the window in swivel mode might have required a different approach or additional clearance checks. However, since tilt mode provided sufficient ventilation, this was not a critical obstacle.

• How I would approach it differently next time:
  – If there is a need for wide or full opening, I would plan in advance to remove or reposition items on the table or move the table itself. That would ensure safe clearance while swinging the sash inward.  
  – I might also verify side‐swing clearance in a more controlled physical test outside the exploration phase (for example, by carefully manipulating the handle and physically monitoring the sash movement) if a pivot mode opening is required.  

Overall, the tilt‐only approach was efficient for ventilation and kept everything around the window safe.
